title: Reading practice: Potholes and a Rain Garden
description: A science explanation of how potholes form and a student’s argument for a rain garden: cause and effect, claims, reasons and evidence.

stimuli.title: Why Roads Get Potholes
paragraphs: A pothole is a hole in a road. Potholes do not appear all at once. They form because of water, cold weather, and heavy vehicles.
First, a road gets small cracks as it gets older. When it rains or snow melts, water runs into the cracks.
Next, the weather turns cold, and the water in the cracks freezes. Water takes up more space when it turns into ice. The ice pushes on the road from the inside, and this makes each crack wider.

When the weather warms up, the ice melts. The melted water drains away and leaves a weak place under the road. Then cars and trucks drive over that weak place. Their heavy wheels break pieces of the road loose, and a hole is left behind.
Workers fix potholes by filling them with new material. Some towns also seal cracks early, before water can get in. Sealing a crack keeps water out, so there is less ice to push the road apart.

stimuli.title: Should Our School Plant a Rain Garden?
paragraphs: Our school has a problem. Every time it rains hard, a big puddle forms beside the parking lot. The water cannot soak into the pavement, so it runs downhill and floods the walkway to the playground. I believe our school should plant a rain garden there.

A rain garden is a shallow hole filled with soil and plants. Water from the parking lot runs into the hole and soaks into the ground slowly. A rain garden would help in three ways. First, it would keep the walkway dry. Second, plants with deep roots would help the water soak into the soil instead of rushing away. Third, the flowers would bring bees and butterflies, and we could study them in science class.

Some people say a rain garden is too much work. However, a garden needs digging only once, and many classes could share the job of pulling weeds. A small amount of work now is better than a flooded walkway every time it rains.
Therefore, I ask the Science Club to vote yes. If you want to help dig on Saturday morning, please wear old shoes, because the soil beside the puddle will still be wet and muddy.

items.stem: Put the steps that make a pothole in order.

items.text: Heavy cars break loose pieces of road, and a hole forms.
Water runs into small cracks in the road.
The ice melts and leaves a weak place under the road.
The water in the cracks freezes and pushes the cracks wider.

items.explanation: Water gets into cracks first. It freezes and widens them, then melts and leaves a weak place, and then heavy vehicles break the road to make a hole.

support.clue: Look for the time words First, Next, and When the weather warms up. Ask which step makes the next step possible.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different process). A puddle in a sandbox dries like this: First, the sun warms the water. Next, some water turns into vapor. Then the vapor rises into the air. Finally, the sand is dry. Each step needs the step before it.

Now put the steps of a pothole in order in the same way.

facts: Water takes up more space when it freezes into ice.
Repeated freezing, melting, and heavy traffic break up damaged road surfaces and make potholes.

items.stem: Why does freezing water make a crack in the road wider?

options.text: The cold air makes the road shrink, so the crack pulls apart.
Water takes up more space as ice, so the ice pushes on the road.
Ice is much heavier than water, so it drags the crack down.
Cars drive faster on cold roads, so they break the crack open.

distractors.a: The passage says the ice pushes the road from the inside. It does not say the road shrinks.
distractors.c: The passage says ice takes up more space and pushes outward. It does not say ice is heavier or that it pulls.
distractors.d: Cars break the road after the ice melts. The crack gets wider while the water is freezing.

items.explanation: The passage says water takes up more space when it turns into ice, so the ice pushes on the road from the inside.

support.clue: Reread the paragraph that begins “Next, the weather turns cold.” Find the sentence about what water does when it turns into ice, and what the ice then does to the road.
support.frame: The crack gets wider because of what happens to the water when it ______, and the ice then ______ the road.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different cause). A bike tire goes flat because a nail makes a small hole, and the air leaks out through the hole. The reason is what the nail does to the tire.

Now explain what the freezing water does to the road in the same way.

misconceptions.c: uses the wrong property of ice

facts: Water takes up more space when it freezes into ice.

items.stem: Match each cause with its effect.

left.text: The ice melts and the water drains away.
Heavy wheels roll over the weak place.

right.text: Pieces of road break loose and a hole forms.
The cracks fill with new road material.
A weak place is left under the road.

items.explanation: Freezing widens the crack. Melting and draining leaves a weak place. Heavy wheels on that weak place break the road and make a hole. Filling the cracks is what workers do, not a result of these causes.

support.clue: For each cause, find the sentence in the passage that tells what happens next. Notice the words “this makes,” “leaves,” and “Their heavy wheels.”
support.model:
Mentor example (a different cause and effect). When the sun shines on a window, the room gets warm. When the curtains close, the room gets dark. Each cause comes first, and each effect is what changes afterward.

Now match each cause to the effect that follows it in the passage.

facts: Water takes up more space when it freezes into ice.
Repeated freezing, melting, and heavy traffic break up damaged road surfaces and make potholes.

items.stem: Which two details tell what people can do about potholes?

options.text: Fill the hole with new material.
Pour hot water on the road to melt the ice.
Seal cracks early so water cannot get in.
Make cars lighter so they do not break the road.

distractors.b: The passage never says to pour hot water on the road.
distractors.d: The passage says heavy wheels break the road, but it does not say to make cars lighter.

items.explanation: The last paragraph says workers fill potholes with new material and some towns seal cracks early.

support.clue: Read the last paragraph. Look for the actions that workers and towns take.
support.frame: Workers ______ potholes, and some towns ______ cracks early.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different topic). A text about a leaky roof says: “Workers patch the hole. Some owners paint the roof early so rain cannot get in.” Two actions are patching the hole and painting early.

Now find the two actions in the last paragraph about potholes.

misconceptions.b: adds an action that is not in the text
misconceptions.d: turns a cause into an action

facts: Towns repair potholes by filling them and can seal cracks to keep water out.

items.stem: Put the parts of the writer’s argument in the order they appear in the text.

items.text: A reply to people who say the garden is too much work
A request to vote yes and help dig
The problem: a big puddle floods the walkway
Three ways a rain garden would help
The claim: the school should plant a rain garden

items.explanation: The writer names the problem, states the claim, gives three reasons, answers a worry, and ends with a request.

support.clue: Read the first and last sentence of each paragraph. Ask what the writer is doing in each paragraph.
support.frame: The writer begins with ______, then states ______, and ends by ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different argument). A review of a lunch menu starts with the claim (the soup is the best choice), then gives two reasons, and ends with a thank-you. Order words and the first sentence of each paragraph show the order.

Now put the parts of the rain garden argument in order in the same way.

items.stem: Sort each sentence: is it a reason for the rain garden, or other information?

tokens.text: Plant roots help water soak into the soil.
Flowers bring bees and butterflies to study in science class.
A big puddle forms beside the parking lot.
Volunteers will dig on Saturday morning.

zones.label: A reason for the rain garden

items.explanation: The writer gives three reasons that start with First, Second, and Third. The puddle is the problem, and the Saturday dig is a plan, so neither one is a reason.

support.clue: A reason answers “Why should we plant a rain garden?” Check which sentences answer that question and which only tell about the problem or the plan.
support.frame: This is a reason because it tells ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different argument). Claim: “We should add a water fountain.” Reason: “Students would drink more water.” Not a reason: “The hallway is near the gym.” A reason answers why the claim is a good idea. A place or a date does not.

Now sort the sentences about the rain garden in the same way.

facts: Plant roots help water move down into the soil.
Flowers can attract bees and butterflies.

items.stem: Which two details are the best evidence that a rain garden would help with the puddle problem?

options.text: The Science Club will vote on the garden at its next meeting.
Water from the parking lot runs into the garden and soaks into the ground slowly.
Flowers in the garden bring bees and butterflies for students to study.
Plants with deep roots help water soak into the soil instead of rushing away.

distractors.a: A vote tells when the club decides, but it does not show how the garden affects the water.
distractors.c: Flowers and bees are a benefit, but they are not about the puddle problem.

items.explanation: The puddle is a water problem. Evidence about water soaking into the ground, and about roots helping it soak in, supports the claim.

support.clue: Ask which details are about water and the puddle. Details about other benefits can be true but do not answer this question.
support.frame: This detail is evidence because it shows that ______ would ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different claim). Claim: “A shade tree would cool the picnic table.” Best evidence: “The tree’s leaves block sunlight, so the table stays shaded.” A weaker detail: “Birds sing in trees.” Best evidence connects directly to the problem in the claim.

Now pick the details that connect directly to the puddle problem.

misconceptions.c: uses evidence for a different benefit

facts: A rain garden collects runoff and lets it soak into the ground.
Plant roots help water move down into the soil.

items.stem: The writer gives instructions to volunteers. Choose the words that explain them.

dropdown.template: The writer asks volunteers to wear old shoes {1} the soil beside the puddle will be {2}. The volunteers will help {3}.

items.explanation: The last sentence says to wear old shoes because the soil beside the puddle will be wet and muddy, and it invites students to help dig on Saturday.

support.clue: Read the last paragraph. Find the word that links the instruction to its reason, find what the soil will be like, and find what the volunteers will do on Saturday.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different notice). A sign at a pool says, “Please walk, because the floor is wet and slippery.” The word “because” connects the instruction to the reason.

Now use the same pattern to explain the instruction to volunteers.
